worksheet.title: Meet Python Turtle
worksheet.subtitle: Ontario Math C3.1 — repeating events, now in typed code
worksheet.learning_goal: I can read a typed loop that makes Bit move again and again.

parts.title: Same loop — now typed
text: You already used a repeat block to make Bit do something many times. Python Turtle does the SAME thing — but you TYPE it instead of dragging blocks.
Here is the repeat you know, and the same idea written in Python. Bit is the turtle that draws.

parts.title: The same thing in Python
parts.output: Bit moves forward 20, three times → 60 steps.

parts.caption: range(3) means do the inside 3 times — Bit makes 3 hops of 20.

parts.title: Read it
parts.prompt: Look at the Python code. range(3) repeats the inside 3 times. How many times does Bit move forward? ______  Each hop is 20, so how far in TOTAL? ______

parts.title: Predict, then run
parts.prompt: You change range(3) to range(5). PREDICT: how many hops, and how far in total? Then run it to check.

parts.title: Write your own
parts.prompt: Make Bit move forward 10, FOUR times. Fill in the two numbers:  for step in range(______):  bit.forward(______)

parts.title: Challenge
parts.prompt: Bit's code is  for step in range(4):  bit.forward(25). How far does Bit travel in total? Show how you worked it out.

parts.title: Big idea
parts.text: range(n) in a Python loop is just like repeat n in blocks — it does the inside n times. Typed code can repeat, exactly like blocks can.

teacher_guide.eyebrow: Teacher Guide · Grade 3 · Intro Python Turtle
teacher_guide.title: Meet Python Turtle
teacher_guide.subtitle: Quick facilitation notes & answer key

parts.title: What this worksheet teaches
parts.text: Students meet typed code for the first time. They read a short instruction that means "repeat 3 times: move forward 20" and work out how many hops Bit makes and how far it travels. It is the same repeat idea they used with blocks — now typed. No coding experience needed.

parts.title: Before you start — showing the drawing (optional)
text: The worksheet shows the typed instructions AND a picture of how far Bit hops, so you can teach straight from the printout — no computer required.

To show it live (optional): open a browser, go to a free "Python turtle" playground (e.g. search "trinket python turtle"), type the few lines from the worksheet, and press Run — a turtle draws it. You only press Run.

parts.title: How to lead it (about 30 minutes)
text: 1. Connect to what they know. Remind them of the "repeat" block from block coding — the typed instruction does the same job.
2. Show it (you do). Read the instruction aloud: "repeat 3 times: move forward 20." Count the hops together — 3 hops of 20.
3. Let them work. Students do Exercises 1–4 (Ex 4 is the stretch), solo or in pairs.
4. Wrap up: the repeat number tells Bit how many times to do the line below it — typed code can repeat, just like the blocks.

parts.title: Answer key (these are the verified correct answers)
text: Exercise 2 — 5 hops; 100 steps in total; the prediction should be 100.
Exercise 3 — the missing numbers are 4 (repeat 4 times) and 10 (move forward 10).

parts.title: If students get stuck — and ways to adjust
text: Watch for: reading "repeat 3" as 4 (counting an extra). It means exactly 3 times.
Make it easier: point at the indented line and say "do this line this many times."
Make it harder: ask the total steps for a "repeat 6, move forward 10" instruction (60).

parts.title: Ontario curriculum link (official wording)
text: C3.1 — solve problems and create computational representations of mathematical situations by writing and executing code, including code that involves sequential, concurrent, and repeating events.
In plain terms: students write and run step-by-step instructions — including a "repeat" instruction — to make something happen.
C3.2 — read and alter existing code, including code that involves sequential, concurrent, and repeating events, and describe how changes to the code affect the outcomes.
In plain terms: students read instructions, change one, and explain what the change did to the result.

parts.title: You'll know it worked when
parts.text: The student reads the repeat instruction as "repeat n times", counts the hops and total distance (Ex 1–2), fills in the repeat line (Ex 3), and works out a total from a typed loop (Ex 4).
